message.content:
**Atomic‑mass units (amu)**  
| Particle | Mass (amu) |
|----------|------------|
| **Proton** | \(m_p \approx 1.007\,276\,466\,88\;\text{amu}\) |
| **Neutron** | \(m_n \approx 1.008\,664\,916\,00\;\text{amU}\) |

These numbers come directly from the most recent CODATA/PDG tables (see e.g., *Particle Data Group*, 2025 edition).  

---

### Diameters (effective “size” of the nucleons)

Because protons and neutrons are composite particles made of quarks bound by gluons, their spatial extent isn’t sharply defined. Experimental determinations usually quote an rms charge radius (\(r_{\rm ch}\)) for the proton and an rms matter radius (\(r_m\)) for the neutron. Converting those into a rough “diameter” gives:

| Particle | Radius (fm) | Diameter (≈ \(2\times r\), fm) |
|----------|-------------|--------------------------------|
| **Proton** | \(r_{ch,p}=0.84093^{+0.00023}_{-0.00024}\,\text{fm}\) | \(\sim 1.68~\text{fm}\) |
| **Neutron** | \(r_{m,n}=0.873^{+0.009}_{-0.010}\,\text{fm}\) | \(\sim 1.75~\text{fm}\) |

*Typical experimental values:*  
- Proton charge radius: \(0.84\!-\!0.87\;\text{fm}\) → diameter ≃ \(1.68\!-\!1.74\;\text{fm}\).  
- Neutron matter radius: \(0.86\!-\!0.90\;\text{fm}\) → diameter ≃ \(1.72\!-\!1.80\;\text{fm}\).

So you can round to roughly **1.7 fm** for each when speaking informally. If higher precision is needed, use the table above along with its stated uncertainties.
